If you’ve ever had a problem with an Apple product and looked online for a solution, there’s a high probability you’ve ended up on the Support Community forums. This is a site owned and operated by Apple, but reliant on the expertise of members of the public, who start threads about ongoing issues (such as the iPhone Duo’s cracked screens) and offer each other advice. You won’t always be able to find a perfect fix there, but it’s a great place to find confirmation that other people are experiencing the same issue as you, and to keep track of the best workarounds currently available.

Sadly, however, the site’s days are officially numbered. At the time of writing, visitors are greeted by a message announcing that Apple Support Community “will permanently close on November 20, 2026,” and directing those seeking guidance to instead head over to Apple’s Support site. For the time being, existing community threads are still available to view, but nothing further can be added. The forums are read-only from now on, and the entire thing will close down in nine days.

Apple doesn’t offer a reason for the decision in its announcement, nor did the company immediately respond to Macworld’s request for comment. So we can only speculate about the rationale.

Apple

One obvious issue with the forums would be the same one encountered by every company operating such a site: The owner has responsibility for the content without having control over it. If news of a hardware problem breaks, forum users will discuss it in a way that carries consequences for Apple’s corporate strategy, potentially widening awareness before the company is ready to release a statement or even seeding misinformation, and disgruntled device owners are unlikely to follow Apple’s desired messaging lines when complaining about the latest thing that has gone wrong. In the thread I linked above, for example, several commenters point out that the screen issue is rare and covered by warranty, but another advises the thread author to stick with conventional iPhones and avoid the Duo for now.

In other words, Apple probably didn’t like the idea of owners googling a problem with their device, seeing the forums in a prominent search ranking and with official Apple branding, and then being exposed to unofficial messaging. It’s a company which is notorious for wanting to control the narrative at all times, and forums are a terrible medium for that.

On the other hand, forums are a brilliant way to generate large amounts of content without having to pay for it, and Apple is about to kiss that goodbye. Apple’s community forums have been around for decades, dating all the way back to 1998. Longtime Apple users will fondly recall browsing Apple Discussion threads before Reddit or Discourse was a thing.

In the vacuum left by Support Community’s absence, however, users will have to look elsewhere. Other sites may see an increase in traffic to their own forums (and Apple will have even less control over the discussions on there) while others with a preference for the official route will visit Apple Support.

But a site curated by in-house writers, even one funded by a multi-trillionaire company like Apple, cannot possibly react as quickly to breaking stories and emerging vulnerabilities as a forum open to the public; it’s not just about manpower, but also about having to get clearance from the PR and legal departments before publishing anything. Apple Support is a more reliable resource in most respects than Support Community, but it cannot perform exactly the same function… unless John Ternus has an AI-based approach in mind.

We’ll update this story if Apple gets in touch with a statement. Until then, make the most of Support Community while you still can.

The more we learn about Apple’s new MacBook Pro, the more we see how different the design is. There’s the display, which has some of the best specs we’ve ever seen; the speakers, which generate more bass when the lid is closed; and the hinge, which is more stable to accommodate taps and pinches. And now we’ve gotten a look at the cooling, which might be the most beautiful of all.

In its announcement of the MacBook Pro, Apple called out its “completely redesigned thermal architecture,” which “enables the same incredible sustained performance of M5 Pro and M5 Max, even in a lighter design, while redirecting warm air away from the display.” That sounds like a lot of fancy words for a whole lot of nothing, but it turns out it’s actually completely reimagined.

A YouTube video by Geekerwan compared the mini-LED MacBook Pro with the new PROLED XDR model using a fog machine. With each MacBook’s fans running, you can clearly see how the internal design disperses the heat: In the old model, heat goes both out and up through the display, while the PROLED pushes the heat toward the back of the device through the hinge.

Geekerwan /YouTube

Pushing the heat out the back is no easy task and required a thorough redesign of the hinge and ventilation system. Not only does the new MacBook Pro do a better job of keeping heat away from the keyboard and display, as Geekerwan explains, but the benefit isn’t simply better cooling capacity when working on the PROLED screen. It also helps disperse heat better when the lid is closed and hooked up to an external monitor. To drive the point home, he tested both models closed and found a massive drop in performance on the older model as a result of thermal throttling.

Geekerwan also found that the fans spun faster and were quieter on the PROLED model. It’s unclear whether that’s due to new hardware or software tweaks, but iFixit’s teardown found the same fan placement under the logic board and nothing particularly noteworthy about the fans themselves.

It’s important to make a distinction between Boot Camp and the virtualization programs that we look at here, such as Parallels Desktop, VMware Fusion and VirtualBox. Instead of creating a virtual machine that allows you to run Mac and Windows apps together at the same time, Boot Camp is a dual-boot system that simply allows you to boot (start) your Mac using either the native macOS or Windows (but not both at the same time).

Thanks to Boot Camp your Mac can act as a straightforward Windows PC, and devote all its processor power and memory to running Windows and your Windows apps. And, crucially, if your Mac has a decent graphics card, it can use the full power of the graphics card to help run your Windows software. That’s definitely the best option for people who need to run high-end graphics software or 3D games, as you get much better performance than when running Windows in a virtual machine.

The disadvantage of using Boot Camp is that you lose access to all your Mac apps while you’re running Windows. If you use Apple Mail for your emails then you’ll need to shut down Windows and Boot Camp, and switch back to macOS every time you want to send or receive an email. And, if truth be told, the current version of BootCamp 6.1 isn’t quite as straightforward to set up as it used to be.

Previous versions of Boot Camp did all the work for you – they would partition your hard drive, install Windows from a normal installer disk, and also install any driver software that you needed so that components such as your graphics card, keyboard and mouse all worked properly within Windows.

Boot Camp does not officially support Windows 11. Running Windows 11 in a virtual machine is a separate option: Parallels Desktop 27 requires Apple silicon, while Intel Mac owners need an earlier compatible release, such as Parallels Desktop 26.

You can’t install Windows from an old installer disk anymore either, so you’ll either have to download a disk image file for Windows – called an ISO file – from Microsoft’s own website, or use your Windows disk to create one. Boot Camp includes driver software for setting up Windows 8 and Windows 10, but if you’re a fan of Windows 7 (which some people prefer for gaming) then you’ll have to hunt around on Apple’s website for the drivers you need and make sure you follow the correct procedure when copying them on to your Boot Camp partition.

Still, if you persevere with all that, you will eventually have Windows running at full speed on your Mac, giving you access to a wide range of Windows software and games that require more power and speed than you can get from using virtual machine technology. How to run Windows on Mac: Apple Silicon vs Intel

If you are still using an Intel-based Mac you can use Apple’s Boot Camp to run Windows. However, in 2020 Apple started using its own processors that are based on Arm architecture rather than the x86 architecture used by Intel. Now every Mac Apple sells has an Apple-made M-series processor. Boot Camp is not available on M-series Macs.

That doesn’t mean that M-series Macs can no longer run Windows, it just means they can’t use Boot Camp and they need the Arm version of Windows.

If you want to run Windows on an M-series Mac. You can choose from virtualization options like Parallels Desktop and VMware Fusion, or compatibility layers like CrossOver and Wine, and even Microsoft’s Windows 365 service. You can read about all of these choices in our group test below as well as our individual reviews.

Our top choice is Parallels Desktop, but all the others have some benefits that may suit you. For example, CrossOver doesn’t actually need a copy of Windows to run Windows apps, and there are even free options like Wine.

What are Apple’s Virtualization.framework tools?

Apple’s Virtualization.framework is a native macOS framework introduced by Apple that lets developers create and manage virtual machines without relying on third-party hypervisors like Parallels or VMware. Unlike Parallels Desktop, it’s not an end-user application. Instead, it’s a set of APIs that developers use to build virtualization software.

VirtualBuddy, a free open-source app for running macOS and Linux VMs is built on Apple’s Virtualization.framework. Other similar options include Tart and OrbStack. These tools are aimed at developers rather than consumers.

Virtualization.framework offers some advantages that developers appreciate, including:

  • Native support from Apple.
  • Lower resource overhead.
  • Integration with macOS security features

However, there are limitations compared to running Parallels and other apps.

FAQ

1.

What is a Virtual Machine?

Virtualization programs such as Parallels Desktop and VMware Fusion run on the macOS, but allow you to create a Virtual Machine (or VM) that mimics the hardware of a Windows PC. This makes it possible to create a VM on your Mac and then install Windows – or another operating system, such as Linux – on the VM. This is a great solution as it allows you to run the Windows apps that you need right alongside your main Mac apps as well. The only disadvantage is that you need a pretty fast Mac with plenty of memory and storage to run Windows as a VM, since it means that your Mac is effectively running two operating systems at the same time.

2.

What is emulation?

Emulation is a process that allows individual Windows applications to run on a Mac without the need for the Windows operating system to be installed. This is achieved through emulation tools, such as Wine and CrossOver, which are typically used by technically proficient users.

3.

Do I need a Windows license?

It depends on which of those two methods you are using. If you are running Windows in a VM then you need a license in order to create a Windows VM on Macs with Apple Silicon processors, and, unfortunately, the less expensive Home edition isn’t supported. However, it is possible to use an existing Windows license if you have one and Microsoft doesn’t differentiate between Windows On Intel and Windows On Arm, see Parallel’s website here.

If you are using emulation you won’t need a copy of Windows.

4.

If you have any AirPods with an H2 chip, it’s time for an update. Apple has released firmware version 9B47 for all AirPods that use the H2. That includes:

  • AirPods Pro 2
  • AirPods Pro 3
  • AirPods 4
  • AirPods 5
  • AirPods Max 2

The previous firmware was 9A348 which added support from Custom EQ and GymKit. A version 9A350 was released just for the AirPods 5, to bring them up to date with those features.

Apple has not yet disclosed the contents of this release on its AirPods Firmware page. It’s likely this is just “bug fixes and performance improvements,” as there aren’t any new iOS or macOS features that should require new firmware.

You can’t update your AirPods firmware manually. But there are steps you can take to check your firmware version and make sure that Apple updates your AirPods sooner rather than later.

How to update AirPods on iPhone, iPad, or Mac

Make sure that your AirPods are in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad, or Mac. Make sure that device is connected to Wi-Fi.

  • Put your AirPods in their charging case and close the lid.
  • Plug in the charging case (plug the USB cable into a power adapter and the charging case).
  • Keep the lid of the charging case closed.
  • Wait at least 30 minutes.
  • Open the lid of the charging case to reconnect your AirPods to your iPhone, iPad, or Mac.
  • Check the firmware version again.

How to check the firmware version of your AirPods

On iPhone or iPad: With your AirPods nearby and the case open, open Settings on your iPhone or iPad. You’ll see your AirPods listed at the top of Settings. Tap that, and scroll down to the bottom of your AirPods settings to see the Version.

On Mac: Open System Settings. Select Bluetooth, then click the (i) next to your connected AirPods. The Version will be listed there, along with other information.

Apple scandals usually revolve around a piece of hardware failing to do what it’s supposed to do: a phone, for instance, that loses connection, or bends in the pocket, or breaks when used normally. So the latest controversy is at least refreshingly different, in that hardware is barely involved at all.

For a couple of weeks now the consumer rights advocate Louis Rossman has been reporting on allegations of malpractice in Apple stores. (You can catch the gist in his latest video on the topic, while a fuller exploration is given in this earlier video.) It’s alleged, specifically, that multiple retail employees in multiple stores have signed up customers to auto-renewing subscription services without obtaining fully informed consent. And worse, that an employee performance metric put in place by Apple management incentivized them to do so.

Apple stores have a system called Connect and Personalize, under which purchasers of a new iPhone, iPad, or Mac scan a QR code to receive a tutorial from a retail employee. This process temporarily unlocks the customer’s account and payment information and shows the employee any free subscription trials for which the customer is eligible. Look, they will then say, you can get three months of Apple One (for example) for free; tap here to start your trial.

Like most services companies, Apple offers free trials not out of a sense of altruism but in the hopes that customers will carry on using the service after the trial ends. They are free to start with, then they auto-renew after a certain amount of time and the customer begins to pay. But whistleblowers claim the auto-renewal part of the deal was not always made clear to customers. Some employees implied that the trials were simply a gift with no strings; others, it is alleged, tapped Accept on their own device and didn’t get consent at all. Needless to say these are very serious allegations. We have contacted Apple for comment and will update this article to include the company’s response if we receive one.

While reports claim the practice is or has been relatively widespread (one tipster told Rossman that they had “confirmed with others that this happens at other stores” and that “many employees [have] admit[ted] to me that they do this”), one defense Apple could offer is that these were rogue employees taking matters into their own hands. That it wasn’t company policy to have employees behave in this way, and that company management is indeed aghast to hear about such goings-on.

But the issue with that defense is that the problem appears to be systemic. Not explicitly, and perhaps not intentionally, but indirectly as a result of employee incentives.

Apple, again like other companies, tracks the performance of its retail employees. Until recently, one metric by which performance was graded was called “services attach rate:” the percentage of device purchasers assisted by the employee who signed up for a subscription service. It’s been reported that employees in at least some stores were set a target of 40 percent. If you help 10 people buy iPads, you should make sure at least four of them sign up to something at the same time.

It isn’t clear what action was taken (or threatened) against employees who failed to meet this target, or whether there was a reward for those who did. But targets affect behavior even in the absence of explicit punishments and rewards. The mere existence of that 40 percent figure tells employees that the company values that specific form of success, and heavily implies that success or failure by this metric will be one of the factors used to determine promotions, redundancies, pay raises, and bonuses. It would be surreally naive to imagine that putting in place a target of this nature wouldn’t encourage employees to hard-sell signups and, in at least a few cases across an organization with more than 100,000 retail staff, bend the rules regarding informed consent.

Apple stopped tracking services attach rate shortly after Rossman’s reporting was published. This might be taken as a tacit acknowledgement that the metric was a bad idea with the potential to incentivise unethical behavior, but Apple claims it’s actually just a coincidence; the company told MacRumors the metric is simply “less relevant during the holiday season.” If that is truly the case, no doubt the metric will be reinstated in the new year.

The company has also reportedly sent internal memos to retail stores reminding employees to make sure they obtain informed consent before signing up customers to subscription trials, and to ensure it is customers, not the employees themselves, tapping the buttons. Again, this may or may not be a coincidence. Stores hire lots of new staff for the holiday season. Maybe it’s just a reminder for the newbies. But the timing is striking, to say the least.

Abuse the user: The dark side of services

Apple’s relentless march into services was one of the great successes of the Tim Cook era.

Overly dependent on the iPhone and trying to plan for the eventual decline of the smartphone market, the company pivoted: instead of just selling hardware, it would focus more and more on selling subscription services to people who own the hardware. This leads to steadier, more predictable recurring revenue and (assuming you own the services content, which Apple does wherever possible) effortless scalability. Building six million iPhone Duos is very difficult and expensive. Making one motor-racing movie is quite difficult and expensive, but distributing it to six million people barely increases your costs at all. At first glance it looks like a business model that’s all upside.

Services certainly have their advantages, and they’ve helped put Apple in a spectacularly strong financial position: this category brought in $30 billion of revenue in the last quarter alone. But selling subscriptions is a murkier business than selling one-off hardware purchases, because there’s more of a disconnect between the best outcomes for buyer and seller.

Look, they will then say, you can get three months of Apple One (for example) for free; tap here to start your trial.
